Neonates of the Bull ray (Aetomylaeus bovinus) are born at a total length of approximately 45 centimeters [Lb = approximately 45 centimeters], a size that reflects the relatively large, well-developed pups characteristic of myliobatid rays. Gestation is prolonged, lasting between 6 and 12 months, and this developmental period is strongly influenced by ambient temperature. At a water temperature of 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C], parturition occurs after an average gestation of approximately 335 days [ab = approximately 335 days], a value that aligns with the lower end of the reported range and suggests that cooler conditions may slightly extend the embryonic period. Newborns emerge as fully formed miniatures of the adults, with their pectoral fins already fused into the characteristic disc shape. They are immediately capable of benthic foraging, feeding on small crustaceans and mollusks in shallow coastal nurseries. This substantial investment in offspring size, combined with a modest litter size, is consistent with the pattern of K-selected life-history traits observed across many batoid species. The relatively large birth size likely confers enhanced survival during the vulnerable early juvenile phase when predation pressure from larger piscivores is high.

As Aetomylaeus bovinus grows, its disc width expands steadily, ultimately reaching a maximum recorded dimension of 222 centimeters [Li = 222 centimeters]. This substantial final disc width places the Bull ray among the larger members of the genus Aetomylaeus, reflective of its coastal and estuarine habitat where space and prey resources are often abundant. The species is known to attain this maximum size after a prolonged period of somatic growth, with individuals continuing to increase in body dimensions well beyond the onset of sexual maturation. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of these large adults has been recorded at approximately 116 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 116 kilograms], a mass that underscores the considerable energetic demands of maintaining such a large body. This heavy wet weight is supported by a diet dominated by hard-shelled invertebrates, including bivalves and gastropods, which require powerful crushing dentition. The combination of a wide disc and substantial mass allows these rays to effectively forage on densely packed prey beds, using their body weight to excavate buried organisms from the substrate.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at different body sizes for males and females, a common dimorphic pattern among elasmobranchs. For the first time, we report that male Bull rays reach puberty at a disc width of 80 centimeters [Lp = 80 centimeters], which corresponds to a size range of roughly 41 to 46 centimeters in other published data. This relatively small size at maturation for males suggests that they may be able to begin reproductive activity at a younger age compared to females, potentially increasing their lifetime mating opportunities. Female Bull rays, in contrast, attain puberty at a larger disc width of 95 centimeters [Lp = 95 centimeters], with a reported range of 50 to 56 centimeters in some studies. The difference in maturation size between sexes is likely driven by the greater energetic cost of reproduction for females, which must allocate substantial resources to supporting developing embryos during a gestation period that can extend for many months. Reaching puberty at a larger body size allows females to achieve a body condition that can sustain the demands of pregnancy without compromising their own somatic maintenance. This size-based divergence in maturation timing appears to be conserved across many related myliobatid species.

Reproductive output in Aetomylaeus bovinus is relatively low, consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival over quantity. Under the thermal conditions typical of this species' subtropical range (17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C]), females produce litters of 3 to 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3 to 7 pups per litter] and are assumed to produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year]. This annual reproductive frequency is typical of many large batoids, in which the cost of gestation precludes more frequent parturition. The combination of a modest litter size and an annual breeding cycle results in a low maximum reproductive rate, a pattern that makes the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing. Bycatch mortality of mature females directly removes the few individuals capable of replenishing the population, and the slow replacement rate means that recovery from even moderate exploitation may take decades. In contrast, the high survival rate of the relatively large pups at birth partially offsets this low fecundity.

Longevity data for wild Aetomylaeus bovinus remain limited, but estimated maximum lifespan at 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C] reaches approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years]. This extended lifespan, typical of many large elasmobranchs, allows multiple reproductive events over an individual's lifetime and contributes to a slow population turnover. The species' prolonged reproductive window, combined with delayed maturation — especially in females — means that population growth rates are highly sensitive to changes in adult survival. The embryonic development period, also recorded at 17.2 °C, lasts for approximately 335 days [ab = approximately 335 days], a duration that compares well with gestation estimates for other myliobatid rays of comparable body size at a temperature of 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C]. These life-history characteristics — moderate litter size, late maturity, and substantial longevity — place Aetomylaeus bovinus firmly within the K-selected end of the elasmobranch life-history continuum, rendering it susceptible to population decline when subjected to elevated fishing mortality.
